rationale: A wins because its sharpest angle turns On's own claim into a reporter-ready accountability story: "On says its shoe subscription \"closes the loop\" — it won't say how big the loop is." B has good bones, especially "On Is a Publicly Traded Company That Just Launched a Subscription Shoe. It Has Not Disclosed the Economics," but it smuggles in unsupported outside evidence. "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" may be true somewhere; it is not in the update, and facts do not get a side entrance.
gaps_in_A: "does the rest of the running category have to follow?" is the weakest angle. The fact block supports On's growth and a national rollout, not category pressure or competitor reaction.
"moving a core product line to this model" overstates the facts. The update says Cyclon is a running shoe subscription, not that this is a core line for On.

"pay monthly to never own their shoes" and "subscription as a bet on product-as-a-service" partially share the same adoption proof. They work only if one stays inside the runner experience and the other stays at category altitude.
gaps_in_B: "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" is an invented supporting claim relative to the supplied update. That is how otherwise-good angles get dirty.

It misses the cleanest accountability headline as its own lane: On says it will close the loop, but disclosed neither recycling rate nor unit economics. B scatters that weakness instead of weaponizing it.
"whether Circular Footwear Is a Viable Business, Not a Brand Bet" is consultant phrasing. The angle is real, but the headline sands off the sharper question: can On prove the loop works?
"without needing On to hand over proof" is too confident. The investor angle still needs price, unit economics, recovery costs, or filing detail before it becomes more than a smart question.
